newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: China top world steelmaker in 1996, U.N. reports.
newsitem.headline: China top world steelmaker in 1996, U.N. reports.

text.p: China took over from Japan as the world's top crude steelmaker in 1996, leading a general surge among Asian producer countries, but there was a sharp slowdown in the European Union, the United Nations reported on Friday.

A survey issued by the U.N.'s Economic Commission for Europe (ECE) said that although the United States showed a marginal production increase, the former communist states of eastern Europe and the ex-Soviet Union were also in decline.

The ECE, which said its figures were estimates based on figures provided by governments around the globe, set world steel production last year at 750.8 million tonnes, 1.2 million or 0.2 percent down on 1995.

Of the total, China accounted for 100.3 million tonnes, putting it top of the global production league for the first time -- partly because of new electric arc furnace (EAF) capacity coming on stream.
At present, ECE experts said, some 65 percent of world steel is made by the more traditional, and costly, blast furnace method, but there is a growing movement to the much cheaper EAF process.

Japan, the 1995 global leader, saw output drop by 2.8 percent in 1996 to 98.7 million tonnes. The 15 EU member states showed an even sharper decline of 5.3 percent from 155.8 million in 1995 to 147.6 million tonnes.

The overall global decline was largely due to stock reductions and weakening economic activity in both Japan and the EU, for both of which 1996 was a period of adjustment after high inventory levels at the end of 1995, the ECE said.

Within the EU, leading producers Germany, Italy and France all saw sharp drops in steel output. Germany was down 5.3 percent to 39.8 million tonnes, Italy down 12.1 percent to 24.4 million and France dropped 2.7 percent to 17.6 million.
Spain also recorded a steep decline of 10.6 percent to 12.3 million tonnes but Britain, with a total of 18.2 million tonnes, increased output by 3.5 percent.

The United States, spurred by overall economic growth with low inflation, saw production increase by 0.7 percent to 94.4 million tonnes. The ECE said the start-up of some mini-mills for flat products had also helped boost the total.
But Canada, the U.N. agency reported, saw a 0.6 percent decline to 14.2 million tonnes.

Apart from Japan, Asian countries showed dynamic growth in steel production with South Korea increasing output by 6.1 percent to 39 million tonnes, India by 8.5 percent to 21.9 million and Taiwan by 10.1 percent to 12.7 million.
The ECE said the surge in all three was largely due to new plants coming on line.
Australia saw a decline of 1.9 percent to 9.1 million tonnes.

Although economic growth continued in the former Soviet-bloc states of eastern and central Europe, high indirect steel imports and a persistent decline in exports led to an overall drop of 9.8 percent in steel output.
The biggest decline was recorded by Poland, the region's major steelmaker, which saw a 13.7 percent drop to 10.2 million tonnes, according to the report.

Russia and Ukraine, the powerhouses of the old Soviet steel industry, returned drops of 4.4 and 2.6 percent to 49 million and 21.7 million tonnes respectively. Overall the former Soviet republics dropped 3.3 percent to 76.2 million.

The ECE said the industry in Latin America saw a 4.3 percent production surge for a total of 49.9 million tonnes, led by strong growth of 14.5 percent in Argentina, to a total of 4.1 million tonnes, and of 8.8 percent in Mexico to 13.2 million.
But Brazil, the region's main producer, returned an increase of only 0.8 percent to 25.3 million tonnes.
